question: A young woman presents to the emergency department with retrograde amnesia for the past 6 hours after a party. Drug-facilitated sexual assault using GHB is suspected. What is the most important IMMEDIATE forensic action?

answers.text: Collect urine and blood samples immediately — GHB's detection window in urine is only 4–8 hours; delay means forensic evidence is permanently lost

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. GHB is rapidly eliminated — detectable in urine for only 4–8 hours and blood for 6–8 hours. Once this window closes, the evidence is gone forever. Immediate specimen collection is the forensic imperative. Crucially, GHB is NOT detected by standard hospital urine drug immunoassays — specific forensic laboratory testing (GC-MS) must be requested.

answers.text: Administer IV flumazenil to reverse the amnestic effects and allow the patient to recall events

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines (GABA-A BZD-site antagonist) but does NOT reverse GHB. GHB acts primarily on GABA-B receptors — there is no clinically available specific antidote. By the time the patient presents, the acute drug effect has already resolved; the amnesia is retrograde and irreversible.

answers.text: Order a standard hospital urine drug screen — GHB will be detected alongside benzodiazepines on routine immunoassay

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Standard hospital urine drug screens (immunoassay panels) test for opioids, benzodiazepines, cannabis, cocaine, and amphetamines. GHB is NOT detected by these routine panels. Specific GC-MS testing at a forensic reference laboratory is required — this must be explicitly requested.

answers.text: Wait for the patient to regain full consciousness and consent before collecting any specimens

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While informed consent is important, in a suspected sexual assault the patient is typically conscious and distressed when presenting. The critical issue is the 4–8 hour detection window — any delay for administrative processes risks losing irreplaceable forensic evidence. Specimen collection is a medical-forensic priority.

overallFeedback.feedback: Three facts about GHB in DFSA: (1) detection window is only 4–8 hours in urine — collect immediately; (2) NOT detected by routine hospital drug screens — request specific forensic testing; (3) no antidote exists (GABA-B mechanism) — management is supportive.

GHB's ultra-short detection window (4–8 hours urine) makes immediate specimen collection the single most time-critical forensic action. Always request specific GHB testing (not routine immunoassay) and document the chain of custody.
